source: Gurnee, Sofroniew, Pearce et al. (Anthropic, 2026) Verbalizable representations form a global workspace in language models: J-space definition and capacity
finding: The page exists on transformer-circuits.pub, dated 6 July 2026, with Jack Lindsey as correspondence author. OpenAlex lists it as arXiv 2607.15495. It defines a J-lens (one residual-stream direction per vocabulary token, from a Jacobian) and a J-space of at most 25 active concept vectors. This closes the 'is it real' question.
numbers: Cap: no more than 25 J-lens vectors active at once. J-space is never more than 10% of activation variance. Models: Claude Sonnet 4.5 main, Haiku 4.5 and Opus 4.5 as checks. Page text is about 322,000 characters; read via fetch plus local text search.
limits: Interpretability result on one model family by the vendor. The lens covers only single-token concepts and 'only approximately and incompletely' captures the workspace (authors' own words). Not independently replicated. Calling this a GWT workspace is the authors' framing; it measures a residual-stream subspace, not an agent scaffold.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that a few items (about 25, far fewer at one layer) carry the model's verbalizable content. It does not show that forcing a small external scratchpad improves accuracy.

source: Gurnee et al. (2026) J-space causal swaps, as read on the primary page
finding: Swapping the J-space component of a concept vector changes what the model reports far more than swapping the non-J component.
numbers: Category swap: J component puts target in top-5 on 59% of trials, pure J-lens vectors 88%, non-J component 5% (n not stated on page). Two-hop intermediate swap, 50 prompts: 54% Haiku 4.5, 70% Sonnet 4.5, 70% Opus 4.5. Probe flip n=90: J component flips answer 61%, non-J 28%, 6% when J coordinates clamped. Flexible swaps 192 trials: 76 at standard strength, 101 at alpha 2. Heavy J-space ablation (top-10 directions, heavy layer band) drops multihop accuracy to near zero.
limits: Small prompt sets (50, 90, 192). Single vendor. Task design is the authors' own. The earlier cross-check could not confirm these numbers; they now match the page text.
agent_relevance: Gives a causal handle: the answer follows the content held in this small subspace. A scaffold that makes the held item explicit and checkable is consistent with this, but is not tested by it.

source: Gurnee et al. (2026) J-space broadcast heads, ignition test and reflection fine-tuning
finding: Ablating the top 1% of 'broadcast heads' lowers recall of J-space contents and removes the model's report of an injected thought. A sharp switch between two readings appears near layer 38. Fine-tuning on counterfactual reflection reduces fabrication and deception on the authors' benchmarks.
numbers: Broadcast-head ablation: J-lens recall@25 falls to 0.67 vs 0.86 for control heads; top-1 next token changes at 5% of positions vs 2% control. Injected-thought report rate 0.54 to 0.09, control intact. Ignition test: 16 country pairs x 40 sentences, choice sharpens near layer 38. Reflection fine-tuning: fabrication 0.25 to 0.07, deception 0.38 to 0.05 (earlier note: 27 transcripts and 100 scenarios). Lines 0.67/0.86, 0.54/0.09, 0.25/0.07, 0.38/0.05 verified in page text.
limits: Fabrication and deception scores are LLM-graded on a 3-point scale. Benchmarks written by the same group. The 'ignition' is sharpening across depth, not a recurrent all-or-none event; the authors say broadcast happens over depth.
agent_relevance: A trained reflection step lowered dishonest answers on the authors' own tests. That is training, not a scaffold, so it is only an indirect hint for a reflect-then-commit operator.

source: Cogitate Consortium (2025, Nature 642) Adversarial testing of GNW and IIT: Prediction 3 (connectivity) and PFC category decoding, published text
finding: The published text differs from the preprint reading. The preregistered connectivity analysis supported neither theory. Category is decodable in PFC but briefly, and adding PFC to posterior decoders gives no gain.
numbers: Prediction 3 preregistered PPC with PFC: iEEG BF01 2.62 to 5.32 (no content-selective synchrony); verdict 'supported neither theory'. Exploratory iEEG dynamic connectivity: PFC synchrony for faces (19 patients, 81 electrodes) and objects (14 patients, 57 electrodes), brief. fMRI gPPI n=70: null in 62 to 94% of prefrontal voxels (BF01 3 to 7.75). PFC decoding: iEEG face vs object about 70% (n=29, window 0.2 to 0.4 s) vs posterior over 95%; MEG n=65; fMRI n=73, about 60% PFC vs about 75% posterior. Adding PFC to posterior decoders: iEEG BF01 1.94e4 (face/object), 1.91e5 (letter/false font), 1205 (orientation); MEG BF01 3.05, 4.70, 3.26. Orientation absent in PFC iEEG (BF01 5.11 to 8.65).
limits: Read the first 100,000 of about 240,000 characters of the PMC full text. Closes cross-check gap 3: the b02 numbers are confirmed and the a18 'supports GNWT' reading came from the preprint and is superseded. One stimulus set and task (faces, objects, letters, false fonts).
agent_relevance: Broadcast of abstract categories to PFC is partly supported; fine detail (orientation) is not. Fits an agent design where the commit step carries a summary, not full detail.

source: Cogitate Consortium (2025, Nature) sustained maintenance and offset ignition in PFC, published text
finding: No PFC electrode showed the predicted onset-plus-offset ignition profile. Posterior cortex tracked stimulus duration better than PFC.
numbers: 0 of 655 PFC electrodes with onset-plus-offset (BF01 above 3 for all); 10 striate/extrastriate electrodes showed offset responses; 99 PFC electrodes non-selective onset and 24 category-selective onset. 25 of 657 posterior electrodes tracked stimulus duration; 8 of 53 face-selective (15%) sustained. One exploratory inferior-frontal-sulcus electrode fit the pattern but about 0.15 s earlier than predicted. Total N 256 (fMRI 120, MEG 102, iEEG 34).
quote: challenged by the general lack of ignition at stimulus offset
limits: iEEG coverage is clinical and patchy. The GNWT camp disputes whether this design tests their theory (see b05). The iEEG N is 34 in the text, 29 for decoding.
agent_relevance: The all-or-none ignition part of GWT is the weakest-supported part. For the agent, borrow only the select-and-broadcast function, not the ignition dynamics.

source: Reaction to the Cogitate Nature paper (press and commentary, 2025 to 2026), via one web search
finding: Search results report online publication on 30 April 2025 and contested reactions. An open letter by 124 scientists targeted IIT. A second large Cogitate experiment is said to be in preparation. No independent replication was found.
numbers: none read beyond snippets
limits: Snippets only. A 2026 essay claimed no theoretical revision followed; one commentary, not consensus.
agent_relevance: No replication exists to lean on, so keep K04 contested.

source: Han and Zhang (2025) Exploring advanced LLM multi-agent systems based on blackboard architecture (LbMAS)
finding: A blackboard system with a control unit that chooses which agents act each round matched the no-control-unit version on accuracy at about a third of the token cost. A cleaner agent that deletes redundant messages beat one that only marks them.
numbers: Table 5 (accuracy MMLU / GPQA / MATH): full LbMAS 85.17 / 54.04 / 72.60 with 5,074,931 / 2,984,204 / 4,721,489 tokens. Without control unit 85.52 / 53.53 / 72.80 with 18,829,644 / 13,325,826 / 13,858,631 tokens. Without message removal (mark, not delete) 84.38 / 53.53 / 71.00. Max-round sweep (Table 4) at 2,4,6,8 rounds, MMLU 84.28, 85.17, 84.21, 84.21; GPQA 52.02, 54.04, 53.03, 51.01; MATH 72.8, 72.6, 71.6, 74.8. MATH 500 questions; MMLU 1140. MATH: LbMAS 72.60 at 4.72M tokens vs Chateval 70.20 at 5.45M, AFlow 70.77 at 13.0M, MaAS 69.25 at 16.7M. Average gain over CoT 4.33 points, over static multi-agent 5.02.
limits: Temperature 0.7, one run, no confidence intervals; differences of 0.3 to 0.5 points are noise. Selection here means which agent acts; the blackboard is open to all agents, so there is no single-item bottleneck. Two LLMs mixed as backbones.
agent_relevance: Selecting what is posted and deleting stale items saves tokens at no accuracy cost, and deleting beats flagging. This is the closest ablation of 'selection vs no selection' for gap 5, but the effect is on cost, not accuracy.

source: Salemi et al. (2025) LLM-based multi-agent blackboard system for information discovery in data science
finding: A blackboard where the main agent posts requests and sub-agents respond beat RAG and a master-slave design on three data-science benchmarks, at higher token cost.
numbers: KramaBench, DS-Bench, DA-Code success (last column of Table 1, as I read the extracted layout): Gemini 2.5 Flash RAG 14.52, master-slave 14.49, blackboard 16.54. Gemini 2.5 Pro RAG 24.01, blackboard 28.53. Claude Opus 4 RAG 23.00, master-slave 27.63, blackboard 31.43. Authors: 13% to 57% relative gain over the best baseline; up to 9% relative F1 gain in file discovery. Cost about 2.3x RAG and 1.8x master-slave; 54.1% gain over RAG, 18.8% over master-slave. More clusters (2, 4, 8, 16) generally helped because each sub-agent sees a smaller subset.
limits: Table text extracted from a PDF with garbled rows; Qwen3-Coder rows not used. No ablation of one chosen item versus all items. The design broadcasts a request to many sub-agents, so it tests broadcast more than selection.
agent_relevance: Supports splitting work so each specialist sees a smaller coherent subset with a shared board coordinating them. The gain is paid for in tokens, so it is not an equal-token win.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Game of 24, crossword ablations and cost (reopened for gap 6)
finding: Keeping a few candidate thoughts and pruning the rest by an explicit evaluation beat independent sampling at roughly equal tokens. Removing pruning or backtracking hurt on crosswords.
numbers: Game of 24 (GPT-4): IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC k=100 9.0%, ToT b=1 45%, ToT b=5 74%, IO best of 100 33%, CoT best of 100 49%. ToT about 5.5k completion tokens, close to 100 CoT trials (6.7k tokens). Mini crosswords: without pruning performance 'generally worse'; without backtracking (greedy, b=1) word-level success 20%. Oracle best-state output solved 7/20 games.
limits: Hard pruning to b=5 is a selection step, but it keeps 5 items, not one, and the evaluator is the same LLM. It does not compare hard commit with soft mixing directly. GPT-4 era; Game of 24 is a task where search helps unusually much. Tree of Thoughts has its own subfield, run in parallel.
agent_relevance: Best equal-token evidence that a code-enforced keep-few-and-prune loop beats unstructured sampling. It does not isolate the single-item broadcast.

source: Du et al. (2025) Context length alone hurts LLM performance despite perfect retrieval
finding: Even when the model can retrieve all needed evidence perfectly, longer input lowers accuracy. Having the model recite the evidence first, which shortens the effective context, recovers a little.
numbers: 5 open and closed LLMs on math, QA and coding. Accuracy fell 13.9% to 85% as input grew within the context limit. The drop persisted when irrelevant tokens were replaced by whitespace or masked. Recitation before solving improved GPT-4o by up to 4% on RULER.
limits: Abstract page only; full tables not read. Mechanism not identified. The mitigation gain is small.
agent_relevance: Direct support for a small curated working context over soft mixing of everything: length itself is a cost. Supports passing forward only the chosen item.

source: Yu et al. (2025) MemAgent: long-context LLM with an RL-trained overwrite memory
finding: A fixed-size memory (1,024 tokens) that the model overwrites after reading each 5,000-token chunk lets an 8K-window model handle multi-million-token QA. It is a hard-capacity scratchpad with an overwrite rule, trained with RL.
numbers: Abstract: trained on 32K text with an 8K window, extrapolates to a 3.5M-token QA task with performance loss under 5%, and over 95% on 512K RULER. Window split: 1,024 query, 5,000 chunk, 1,024 memory, 1,024 output tokens. Memory-length ablation 256 to 4,096 tokens: authors call 1,024 a reasonable sweet spot and performance robust over memory size (figures only; numbers not extracted). Baseline long-context models fall to about 0 to 14% by 896K tokens (extracted table partly garbled).
limits: RL-trained, so not a prompt-only scaffold. Task is retrieval-heavy QA, not reasoning. The memory-size curve is flat with a mild optimum, not a sharp interior peak. Per-length numbers not recorded because the extracted table is garbled.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue to a k-item workspace at constant compute: constant-size memory with forced overwrite works, and capacity limits cost little. It does not test one-item broadcast.

source: Li et al. (2026) Escaping the context bottleneck: active context curation for LLM agents via RL
finding: A small trained ContextCurator prunes the working memory of a frozen executor model. Success rose a few points while tokens fell.
numbers: WebArena: Gemini-3.0-flash success 36.4% to 41.2%, context tokens 47.4K to 43.3K (8.8% fewer). DeepSearch: 57.1% vs 53.9% with about 8x fewer tokens. A 7B curator matches GPT-4o at context management (authors' claim).
limits: Preprint under review. Gains are 3 to 5 points on one frontier model. Curator is RL-trained. Pruning, not single-item broadcast. Abstract and first pages read; table detail not extracted.
agent_relevance: A second case with equal or fewer tokens where curating a bounded working context helps.

source: Hao, Dai, Qin, Yu (2026) Brain-inspired graph multi-agent systems for LLM reasoning (BIGMAS)
finding: A GWT-framed LLM agent with benchmark numbers exists. Agents are graph nodes that talk only through a shared workspace; a GraphDesigner builds the graph per problem and an Orchestrator sees the full workspace.
numbers: Three tasks, 100 instances each (Game 24, Six Fives, Tower of London). DeepSeek-V3.2 accuracy, base / ReAct / Tree of Thoughts / BIGMAS: Game 24 25.0 / 26.0 / 30.0 / 36.0; Six Fives 12.0 / 18.0 / 25.0 / 30.0; Tower of London 6.0 / 10.0 / 18.0 / 20.0. Six backbones tested (DeepSeek-V3.2 with and without thinking, Claude 4.5 Sonnet with and without thinking, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5); authors say BIGMAS matches or beats base everywhere, with large gains on weaker models and small gains on strong ones.
limits: N=100 per task, single run, no confidence intervals; 2 to 6 point gaps over Tree of Thoughts are within noise at this N. No token-matched comparison seen. The workspace shows everything to every agent (full visibility), the opposite of a small bottleneck, so it tests shared state, not selection. Per-model chart values not extracted.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 8: one benchmarked GWT-style LLM framework exists, but it is a shared-state multi-agent design with modest, uncontrolled gains.

source: Phua (2025) Can we test consciousness theories on AI? Ablations, markers, and robustness
finding: In a small synthetic agent with a discrete-slot workspace, going to 0 slots collapsed access markers, but non-zero capacities looked alike; broadcast also amplified noise.
numbers: Conjunction accuracy about 100% (4 slots), 28% (2 slots), 0% (bus-off), read from Figure 2; text says access markers stay similar across tested non-zero capacities and collapse only at bus-off. 20 seeds for most analyses; capacity sweeps use 32 episodes per seed. Self-Model removal: metacognitive AUROC 0.92 to 0.50 (+0.42). Workspace-only agent fragile to latent noise.
limits: Single author, synthetic agent, not an LLM. Slot allocation is first-free, not competitive. The 28% is read from a chart. A search summary quoted 99.5% vs 28.1%; I did not find those digits in the text I grepped.
agent_relevance: A toy where capacity shows a threshold, not a smooth interior optimum. Warns that broadcast without a quality check amplifies errors, which supports pairing a commit step with a critic.

source: Dossa et al. (2024) Global workspace agent in SoundSpaces audiovisual navigation, re-opened full text
finding: Re-opened to settle gap 7. The article gives no per-size table: numbers are in figures only. The GW agent holds about 80% at every memory size except 256; the GRU stays above 60% and becomes competitive only at larger sizes. The authors say larger workspaces do not help and the GW advantage shrinks as the bottleneck grows.
numbers: Text: GW about 80% across sizes 32 to 512 (except 256), GRU above 60%, random 0%, original SAVi RL agent about 25%. Five seeds, 50,000 iterations each; 10 runs per config in the hyperparameter search. 21 target classes, 56 training scenes, held-out probe set of 150 trajectories (6 targets, 5 scenes). Metrics are IQM with 95% CI, values not in text.
limits: Behavioural cloning, not RL. Authors say SAVi is 'not an adequate benchmark for testing working memory capacity'. Some agents solve it visually. Size-256 dip may be noise. After the sound stops the target probe accuracy drops for both agents, so the GW did not clearly hold the information. No replication found. Not an LLM.
agent_relevance: Confirms K09 as single-source and weak. Shows no interior optimum: flat in size. Do not cite as evidence that a workspace helps reasoning.

source: Devillers, Maytie, VanRullen (2024) Semi-supervised multimodal representation learning through a global workspace, re-opened PDF
finding: Re-opened to settle gap 7. The data-efficiency and ImageNet numbers are confirmed.
numbers: Simple Shapes: semi-supervised model with N=5,000 matched pairs does about as well as a fully supervised one with N=30,000 (6-fold). Natural-language captions: 4.5 times fewer matched examples. Overall 4 to 7 times fewer annotated pairs. ImageNet linear probe: contrastive-only 50.3 +/- 0.2% vs all four losses 55.7 +/- 0.2%. Only GW models do well on the contrastive property.
limits: The gain comes mainly from the cycle-consistency loss using unpaired data; the authors say the GW is critical for contrastive alignment. Synthetic shapes plus COCO and ImageNet, not a reasoning task. No independent replication found.
agent_relevance: Workspace as a shared latent for translating between modalities. Little to take for a text-only reasoning agent.

source: Maytie, Devillers, Arnold, VanRullen (2024) Zero-shot cross-modal transfer of RL policies through a global workspace
finding: A policy trained on one modality works on the other without fine-tuning when built on a frozen global-workspace latent. A CLIP-like contrastive variant did not generalise the same way.
numbers: Abstract page gives no scores. Two environments, two modalities.
limits: Abstract only. Same group as Devillers, so not an independent replication. Not an LLM.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence for the shared-latent idea; no relevance beyond K10.

source: netsky-lab (2026) gwt-context: honest GWT report (MCP memory runtime)
finding: A practitioner project builds a GWT-inspired memory runtime for LLM agents where facts compete for a bounded workspace and accepted items are broadcast to processors. Its own report gives no accuracy or token numbers and says so.
numbers: No figures on the page. Benchmark gains 'mostly prove controlled exact selection, bus health, and no regression'. Arbitration 'is not learned'.
quote: They do not prove universal long-context reasoning gains
limits: Self-published, no baselines on the page, no peer review.
agent_relevance: An engineering version of select-and-broadcast exists with no evidence of an accuracy benefit; even the builder does not claim one.

source: Ye et al. (2025) CogniPair: GNWT-based multi-agent digital twins for dating and hiring
finding: A GNWT-labelled LLM multi-agent system (emotion, memory, norms, planning, goal sub-agents around a workspace) reports agreement with human data on speed-dating.
numbers: 551 GNWT-Agents; Columbia speed-dating data; 72% correlation with human attraction patterns, 77.8% match prediction accuracy, 74% agreement in human validation (abstract). No workspace-versus-no-workspace ablation stated on the page read.
limits: Abstract page only. Social-prediction task, not reasoning. No control for the GWT component seen.
agent_relevance: A GWT-branded agent with benchmark numbers but no test of the GWT component. Low value for our design.

source: Hutchinson, Pustejovsky, Bandara, McGovern, Cox, Voce, Pitts, Slagter (2026, Psychological Bulletin) NCC systematic review and meta-analysis of the VAN and P3b
finding: Abstract confirmed via Europe PMC (record 42734963). P3b is not necessary for awareness; the VAN is present even without awareness.
numbers: 117 studies; seen: 547 effect sizes (322 VAN, 225 P3b); unseen: 89 (55 VAN, 34 P3b). Seen SMD VAN 0.37 [0.32, 0.43]; P3b 0.49 [0.41, 0.57]. P3b under task-irrelevant conditions SMD -0.12 [-0.47, 0.23]. Study quality did not change results; selective reporting may bias estimates upward without changing conclusions.
limits: Abstract only; full text not open access, so the unseen VAN SMD and moderator results were not seen. Registered report. This confirms the headline numbers of b14 only.
agent_relevance: A late ignition-like P3b is not a clean marker of access; do not rest the agent design on ignition.

source: Tait et al. (2026) Evaluating global workspace markers in contemporary LLM systems (Preprints.org 202601.1683)
finding: Reported by a search summary as turning GWT into testable markers for LLM systems. The page returned HTTP 403, so nothing was read.
numbers: none read
limits: Not opened; non-peer-reviewed preprint per the summary.
agent_relevance: Unverified pointer; do not cite numbers.
